name: CSS
description: The cascade, the box model, layout systems and the details that feel designed.

lessons.title: Selectors and the cascade
lessons.summary: How a browser decides which rule wins, and why yours sometimes loses.
objectives: Read a CSS rule: selector, property, value
Predict which declaration wins when two rules collide

sections.body: CSS is a list of claims, and claims conflict

A stylesheet is a set of statements: “every element with class `card` gets this background”, “every `h2` gets this colour”. Each statement has a **selector** that picks elements and a **declaration block** that describes them. Nothing executes in order like a program — the browser collects every matching claim and then decides which one wins.

That decision is the cascade. It is the part of CSS that people find mysterious, and it is completely mechanical once you know the three tie-breakers: importance, specificity, then source order. When a rule “doesn't work”, it is almost never ignored — it is being outranked.
Anatomy of a rule

sections.caption: Two rules: one class selector, one element selector

items: `.card` selects every element with `class="card"`. The dot is part of the selector, not the class name.
`h2` selects every `<h2>` on the page. Convenient, but it means one edit can move a hundred elements.
Properties are `kebab-case`; values are typed — lengths, colours, keywords, functions like `rgb()` or `calc()`.
One typo in a property name silently disables that declaration. The browser does not warn you, it just moves on.

sections.body: Who wins: specificity

Specificity is a score. An element selector (`h2`) counts 1. A class, attribute or pseudo-class (`.card`, `[data-theme]`, `:hover`) counts 10. An id (`#main`) counts 100. Inline `style="…"` beats all of them, and `!important` beats even that.

Compare scores left to right, like a three-digit number: a rule with one class and one element (11) beats a rule with two elements (2), and loses to a rule with two classes (20). When the scores are exactly equal, the rule that appears later in the stylesheet wins — which is why import order matters, and why a stylesheet loaded after yours can override you.

sections.caption: Specificity, not position, decides first

sections.title: !important is a debt with interest
sections.body: Every `!important` you add forces the next developer to add another one to beat it. If you need it, the specificity structure is wrong — usually a missing class on the element you are trying to style.
Prefer classes, and read the inspector

Element selectors are right for base typography — the default look of `body`, `h1`, `a`. Anything you style deliberately should hang off a class, because a class selector scores the same everywhere and does not depend on the surrounding markup.

Your fastest debugging tool is the browser inspector: it lists every declaration that matched, strikes through the ones that lost, and shows the winning rule's file and line. Learn to read that panel and specificity stops being guesswork.
Check yourself

items: Two rules both set `color` on the same element, one with `.card p` and one with `.card .body`. Which wins?
Why does a rule at the bottom of your file sometimes lose to a rule at the top?
What is the cost of fixing a conflict with `!important`?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Selector picks, declaration block describes.
Tie-breakers: importance, then specificity, then source order.
Element 1, class 10, id 100.
Style with classes; reserve ids for anchors and JavaScript hooks.

drills.prompt: Which selector wins when three rules target the same element?
drills.explain: Specificity ranks id beats class beats element: 1-0-0 against 0-1-0 against 0-0-1. The id rule wins even when written first.
hints: Count ids, classes, elements.
The id column is the strongest.

drills.prompt: Target every element with the class `card`.
drills.explain: A leading dot targets a class. Without the dot you are targeting an element named `card`, which does not exist.
hints: Classes start with a punctuation mark.
It is not a hash.

drills.explain: `b` is not a colour value. The declaration is dropped and the element falls back to an inherited colour.
hints: Colours are hex or named.
One value is a single letter.

exercise.brief: Give `.card` a warm surface (`#fffdf8`), a 12px radius, 24px of inner space and a hairline border (`1px solid #e3e0d6`). Then colour `.title` with `#14150f`.

quiz.explain: IDs win over classes, and classes win over element selectors.

quiz.explain: With equal specificity, later source order wins — which is why import order matters.

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.summary: Every element is a box. Learn what is inside it and what pushes it around.
objectives: Distinguish content, padding, border and margin

sections.body: Everything is a rectangle

Every element renders as a box made of four layers, from the inside out: **content**, **padding**, **border** and **margin**. Content is the text or image. Padding is space inside the border that takes the element's background. Border is the visible edge. Margin is empty space outside, pushing other boxes away.
Almost every “why is this 20px too wide” problem is one of these four layers doing something you did not expect. Once the box model is second nature, layout stops feeling like guesswork.
The one line that fixes width forever

sections.caption: 320px means 320px

items: By default `width` measures the content only. Add 24px padding and a 2px border on each side and the box renders 320 + 48 + 4 = 372px wide.
`box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` include padding and border, so the box stays exactly 320px and the content shrinks to fit. This is what you want in 99% of cases.
Padding is inside the border and inherits the background colour; margin is outside and always transparent.
Vertical margins between siblings **collapse**: a 24px bottom margin and a 32px top margin become 32px, not 56px. Padding does not collapse.

sections.body: Margin collapse, the classic surprise

Collapsing is why the gap between two paragraphs is not the sum of their margins, and why a child's top margin can escape its parent and push the whole container down. Three things stop it: padding or a border on the parent, `overflow` other than `visible`, or a flex/grid parent. If a margin seems to be applied to the wrong element, suspect collapse first.
Width, max-width and overflow

`width` is a demand; `max-width` is a limit. A card with `width: 480px` will overflow a 360px phone and cause a sideways scrollbar. The same card with `max-width: 480px; width: 100%` fits everywhere and still stops growing on a desktop. Prefer `max-width` plus `min-width: 0` on flex children, which is the other common source of stubborn overflow.

sections.title: Why the universal reset
sections.body: `box-sizing: border-box` on `*, *::before, *::after` is the one reset worth memorising. It makes every width in your stylesheet mean the same thing, and it costs two lines.
Check yourself

items: A box has `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px`. How wide is it with and without `border-box`?
Two paragraphs have `margin-bottom: 40px` and `margin-top: 16px`. What is the gap?
Why does `max-width` survive a narrow screen when `width` does not?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Content, padding, border, margin — in that order.
`border-box` everywhere, set once on `*`.
Margins collapse vertically; padding never does.
Prefer `max-width` to `width` for anything responsive.

drills.prompt: Which property adds space inside an element, between content and border?
drills.explain: `padding` is inside the border; `margin` is outside it. That distinction is what makes box maths predictable.
hints: Margin is outside.
Seven letters.

drills.explain: `border-box` folds padding and border into the declared width, so 200px is the size you actually see. Margin stays outside.
hints: Margin is never inside the box.
The border is inside the declared width.

drills.prompt: A box is 100px wide with 10px padding and `box-sizing: content-box`. How wide is it on screen?
drills.explain: With `content-box` the padding is added on top: 100 + 10 + 10 = 120px. That is exactly the surprise `border-box` removes.
hints: Padding applies on both sides.
Add, do not subtract.

exercise.brief: Give `.box` a fixed 320px width, 24px padding, a `2px solid #1e4b3a` border and `box-sizing: border-box`. The rendered box should stay exactly 320px wide.
exercise.markup:
Packing list

Notebook, thermos, and a jacket that can take rain.

checks.label: The border is 2px of pine green

hints: Set `box-sizing: border-box` on `.box` if you are not using a reset.
`border: 2px solid #1e4b3a` sets width, style and colour together.

quiz.prompt: An element is 200px wide with 20px padding and a 1px border, default box-sizing. How wide does it render?
quiz.explain: 200 + 20 + 20 padding + 1 + 1 border = 242px. That is the surprise border-box removes.

quiz.prompt: Which layer shows the element's background colour?
quiz.explain: Backgrounds paint under the content and the padding, but not the margin.

lessons.title: Colour, type and rhythm
lessons.summary: The handful of properties that decide whether text feels designed.
objectives: Set a readable measure for body text
Build hierarchy with size, weight and colour
Use letter-spacing and case for small labels

sections.body: Most of your interface is text

Four decisions do most of the work of making a page feel designed: the typeface, the size scale, the line-height, and the measure — how wide a line of text gets. Get those right and the page reads as calm even before you add colour. Get them wrong and no amount of gradient will save it.
A body style worth reusing

sections.caption: Body, lead and label — three levels from one scale

items: A line of body text reads best between 45 and 75 characters. `max-width: 62ch` is a reliable target; `ch` is the width of a zero, so it scales with the font size instead of being frozen in pixels.
Line-height 1.4–1.7 for paragraphs; tighter (1.05–1.25) for large headings, where the extra space looks like a mistake.
Build hierarchy with size **and** weight **and** colour, not just size. A 15px semibold label and a 15px regular body can coexist if the weight and colour differ.
Two typefaces is plenty: one for display, one for text. A third is usually a decision you will regret at load time.

sections.body: Why the small label needs letter-spacing

Uppercase text loses the ascenders and descenders that help the eye separate letters, so it needs help. A tiny amount of tracking — `letter-spacing: 0.08em` — plus a smaller size and a muted colour turns “MY ACCOUNT” from shouty into a quiet label. Below about 12px, uppercase text becomes hard work for everyone.

sections.title: Contrast is not optional
sections.body: Body text should hit at least 4.5:1 against its background. Muted grey on cream is a classic failure: `#7c7a71` on `#f5f2ea` is about 3.4:1 — pretty, and unreadable for a lot of people in daylight.
Space is part of the type

Proximity tells the eye what belongs together. Give a heading more space above it than below, and it groups with the paragraph it introduces. Give two unrelated blocks the same gap and the page reads as a list of equal things, which is rarely what you mean.
Pick a spacing scale — 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48 — and use only those values. Random spacing is the difference between a layout that feels deliberate and one that feels almost right.
Check yourself

items: Why is `max-width: 62ch` better than `max-width: 700px` for body text?
When should line-height go down rather than up?
Name two ways to make a label feel secondary without shrinking it.

sections.body: What to remember

items: Typeface, scale, line-height, measure — fix those four first.
45–75 characters per line, `ch` units.
Hierarchy comes from weight and colour as much as size.
Use a spacing scale; avoid one-off values.

drills.prompt: Set body text to a comfortable line height.
drills.explain: A unitless line-height multiplies the font size, so it scales with every element. 1.5 to 1.7 is the readable range for body copy.
hints: Unitless scales.
Somewhere between 1.5 and 1.7.

drills.prompt: Why prefer `rem` over `px` for type sizes?
options: It respects the user's root font-size setting
drills.explain: `rem` is relative to the root font size, so a user who raised their default gets larger text everywhere. `px` ignores that preference.
hints: Think about accessibility settings.
The r in rem means root.

exercise.brief: Style the article: `.lead` at 18px in `#4a4a44` with `max-width: 62ch`, `.eyebrow` uppercase with `letter-spacing: 0.08em`, and give `.title` a `font-weight` of 600.

checks.label: The lead paragraph is muted grey

hints: `letter-spacing: 0.08em` is relative to the font size, so it scales.
`text-transform` changes the rendered case, not the HTML.

quiz.prompt: Why is `max-width: 62ch` better than `max-width: 700px` for body copy?
options: It scales with the font size and caps characters per line
quiz.explain: `ch` is tied to the font, so the measure stays readable when the user increases text size.

quiz.prompt: Which line-height suits a paragraph of body text?
quiz.explain: Around 1.5–1.7 gives comfortable line spacing for prose. Tight values are for headings.

lessons.title: Flexbox, properly
lessons.summary: One axis, total control. The layout tool you will reach for every day.
objectives: Understand main axis vs cross axis
Space items with gap instead of margins

sections.body: One axis, total control

Flexbox lays out children along a single axis. Set `display: flex` on the parent, and the children become items you can distribute, align and reorder. The mental model that unlocks it: there is a **main axis** (the direction items flow) and a **cross axis** (perpendicular to it). Every property acts on exactly one of them.

By default the main axis is horizontal, so `justify-content` spaces items left-to-right and `align-items` moves them up and down. Add `flex-direction: column` and the two swap roles — the single most common source of confusion.
A toolbar, in five lines

sections.caption: Align on the cross axis, distribute on the main axis

items: `justify-content` distributes along the main axis: `flex-start`, `center`, `flex-end`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.
`align-items` positions on the cross axis. `stretch` is the default, which is why children mysteriously become full height.
`gap` only applies *between* items — no trailing margin on the last one, no negative-margin hacks.
`flex: 1` lets an item grow into leftover space; `flex: 0 0 auto` keeps it at its natural size. `flex: 1` on a child is how you make a search field fill the middle of a header.

sections.body: Growing and shrinking

`flex` is shorthand for three values: grow, shrink, basis. `flex: 1` means “start from 0, take an equal share of the free space”. `flex: 1 1 auto` means “start at your natural size, then share the leftovers”. The difference shows up when items have different content lengths — and it is why one item sometimes eats the whole row.

Items also refuse to shrink below their content by default. A long word or an unbreakable URL will push a flex row wider than its container. The fix is `min-width: 0` on the item that is overflowing, not a smaller font.

sections.title: flex-wrap changes the rules
sections.body: Once items wrap, `justify-content` distributes each line and `align-content` distributes the lines themselves. If a wrapped row looks like two unrelated rows, that is the property you are missing.
When not to use flexbox

For centring a single thing, `display: grid; place-items: center` is shorter and more reliable. For a row of controls, a toolbar or a media object (avatar plus text), flexbox is still the right tool. And if you are fighting flexbox to control both rows and columns, the layout wants grid.
Check yourself

items: With `flex-direction: column`, which property moves items horizontally?
Why does a long unbroken URL break a flex row, and what fixes it?
What is the difference between `flex: 1` and `flex: 1 1 auto`?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Main axis from `flex-direction`, cross axis perpendicular.
`justify-content` main, `align-items` cross.
Space with `gap`, never margins.
`min-width: 0` rescues overflowing flex children.

drills.prompt: Which property aligns items along the main axis of a flex container?
drills.explain: `justify-content` works on the main axis; `align-items` works on the cross axis. In a row, main is horizontal.
hints: Main axis, not cross axis.
It is the one with 'content'.

drills.prompt: Order a toolbar that pushes its last button to the right.
drills.explain: `margin-left: auto` on a flex child eats the free space on that side, which pushes everything after it to the far end.
hints: The container comes first.
Auto margins absorb free space.

drills.prompt: Which property sets spacing between flex items without margins?
drills.explain: `gap` is applied by the container and never adds space on the outer edges, which is why it replaced margin hacks.
hints: Three letters.
It replaced a long-standing hack.

exercise.brief: Turn `.bar` into a flex row with 24px gaps, vertically centered items, and the links pushed to the right edge with `justify-content: space-between`.
exercise.markup:
Zuno
Learn Playground Pricing

checks.label: The bar is a flex container
The brand and links sit at opposite ends
There is a 24px gap between the two groups
The link list is also a flex row

hints: `align-items: center` centers on the cross axis, which is vertical in a row.
`space-between` pushes the first item to the start and the last to the end.

quiz.prompt: In `flex-direction: row`, which property aligns items vertically?
quiz.explain: The main axis is horizontal, so vertical alignment is the cross axis: align-items.

quiz.prompt: Why prefer `gap` over margins between flex items?
options: It only adds space between items, never at the ends
Margins do not work in flexbox
quiz.explain: gap spaces the gaps, not the outer edges — no :last-child hacks required.

build.blurb: A flex row with real gaps, centred items and the links pushed to the far edge.

lessons.title: Grid and responsive design
lessons.summary: Two-dimensional layout, then make it survive a 320px screen.
objectives: Create a responsive card grid with auto-fit

sections.body: Two dimensions at once

Flexbox distributes along one axis. Grid defines rows **and** columns and places items into the resulting cells. That makes grid the right tool for page layouts and card collections, and flexbox the right tool for rows of controls.

The most useful grid pattern in day-to-day work is a card grid that reflows by itself, with no media query at all: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))`. Learn that line and you will use it for the rest of your career.
A grid that fits itself

sections.caption: As many 240px columns as fit, sharing the leftover space

items: `repeat(auto-fit, …)` creates as many columns as fit and collapses the empty ones. `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks instead, which leaves gaps at the end of a short row.
`minmax(240px, 1fr)` means “never narrower than 240px, but grow to share the free space”.
`1fr` is a share of the free space, not a fixed size — three `1fr` columns are equal only because they get the same share.
`gap` works for rows and columns, so you rarely need margins between grid items.

sections.body: When a media query is actually needed

A grid that reflows covers most of it. Reach for a media query when the *structure* changes, not just the count: a sidebar that moves below the content, a table that becomes a list of cards, a nav that becomes a drawer. Write the small-screen layout as the base, then add complexity upward with `@media (min-width: 720px)`. That is mobile-first, and it produces less override code than the reverse.

sections.caption: One column by default, sidebar above 960px

sections.body: The 320px test

Open the device toolbar, set the width to 320px and scroll. If the page moves sideways, something has a fixed width wider than the viewport — a `width`, a long word, a wide table, an image without `max-width: 100%`. Finding that element takes a minute; shipping without checking costs you every phone user.

sections.title: minmax(0, 1fr) in sidebars
sections.body: `1fr` is shorthand for `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, and that `auto` minimum refuses to shrink below its content. Long code blocks or URLs then blow out the layout. Writing `minmax(0, 1fr)` is the fix you will need sooner or later.
Check yourself

items: `auto-fit` versus `auto-fill` — what differs visually?
Why can a `1fr` column still overflow?
What should be in the base styles versus inside a media query?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Grid for two dimensions, flexbox for one.
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` is the card-grid line.
Mobile-first: base styles for small, media queries add structure.
Test at 320px before you ship.

drills.prompt: Make three equal columns that collapse to one on narrow screens.
drills.explain: `repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))` gives three equal tracks that can shrink below their content. On small screens one track stacks them.
hints: How many columns?
One column is 1fr.

drills.prompt: What does `1fr` mean in a grid template?
options: One share of the leftover space
drills.explain: `fr` is a fraction of the free space after fixed tracks and gaps are taken out. Two `1fr` tracks are equal whatever the viewport.
hints: It is a share, not a size.
Free space gets divided.

exercise.brief: Make `.grid` a responsive grid: three equal columns at desktop width, 16px gaps, using `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))`. Add a `@media (max-width: 640px)` block that sets the grid to a single column.

checks.label: Three columns are laid out at this width
A media query handles small screens

hints: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` is one declaration — no media query needed for the reflow.
The media query is a separate block, not nested inside `.grid`.

quiz.prompt: What does `1fr` mean in a grid track?
options: One fraction of the available free space
quiz.explain: fr distributes the leftover space after fixed sizes and gaps are accounted for.
auto-fit collapses empty tracks so the remaining items stretch; auto-fill keeps them reserved.

lessons.title: Custom properties and theming
lessons.summary: Design tokens, one override, and a theme switch with no JavaScript.

sections.body: Variables that live in the cascade

A custom property is a value you name once and read everywhere. Unlike a preprocessor variable, it is resolved by the browser at runtime and it **inherits** like any other property. That inheritance is the whole trick: a theme is just a different set of values on a parent element.
Tokens on :root, themes on a scope

sections.caption: Components read tokens; themes only change values

items: Declare tokens on `:root` so every element can inherit them.
A `[data-theme="dark"]` scope overrides only the values. `.panel` never needs to know a theme exists.
Because custom properties inherit, a theme can be applied to one section of the page, not just the whole document.
`var(--surface, #ffffff)` supplies a fallback so a component still renders if the token is missing.

sections.body: Name by role, not by value

`--surface` and `--ink` survive a redesign; `--grey-100` does not. The day you make the palette warm, the name lies and every future reader has to check the value. Name tokens after the job they do — surface, ink, muted, accent, line — and the stylesheet becomes readable.
Theming without duplicating rules

The payoff is that dark mode stops being a second stylesheet. Set `data-theme="dark"` on `<html>` from a small script (or from a user preference), let the tokens change, and every component follows. Add `color-scheme: light dark` so form controls and scrollbars match.

sections.caption: Respect the system setting, allow an explicit override

sections.title: Do not animate every token
sections.body: Transitioning custom properties that feed layout can trigger expensive repaints. Animate the concrete property (`background-color`, `color`) or a transform instead.
Check yourself

items: Why does a theme on a `<section>` work without any extra CSS?
What breaks if you name a token `--grey-100`?
When is a fallback value worth writing?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Custom properties are runtime values that inherit.
Tokens on `:root`, theme overrides on a scope.
Name by role: surface, ink, muted, accent, line.
`color-scheme` keeps native controls consistent.

drills.prompt: Read a custom property with a fallback.
drills.explain: The name includes the two dashes. The second argument to `var()` is the fallback used when the property is undefined.
hints: Custom property names start with two dashes.
It matches the name in `:root`.

drills.prompt: Where must a custom property be declared so it can be overridden per section?
options: On any selector — the cascade decides the winner
drills.explain: Custom properties are inherited, so declaring them on a section overrides the `:root` value for everything inside it. That is the whole point of theming.
hints: They cascade like any other property.
`:root` is just the most common place.

exercise.brief: Declare `--surface` and `--ink` on `:root` (light values `#ffffff` / `#14150f`), override them under `[data-theme="dark"]` (`#16181c` / `#f2efe6`), and make `.panel` use `var(--surface)` and `var(--ink)` with 24px padding.

Light

Dark

checks.label: The panel reads tokens with var()
Dark theme text is warm off-white

hints: The `[data-theme="dark"]` block only overrides values — do not repeat `.panel` inside it.
`var(--surface)` is the syntax; the fallback form is `var(--surface, #fff)`.

quiz.prompt: Why does a theme override work without touching component rules?
options: Because var() is evaluated at runtime by JavaScript
Because custom properties inherit and are resolved on each element
quiz.explain: Inheritance carries the value down; `var(--surface)` resolves against the nearest ancestor's value.

quiz.prompt: Which token name survives a rebrand best?
quiz.explain: Names that describe the role keep meaning when the palette changes.

lessons.title: Motion and polish
lessons.summary: Transitions that feel physical, and the accessibility guard everyone forgets.
objectives: Animate only transform and opacity for performance

sections.body: Motion is feedback, not decoration

A hover lift tells you a card is interactive. A 900ms fade tells you the designer had time on their hands. Good motion answers a question the user already has — did that work, where did it come from, what changed — and then gets out of the way.
Two properties worth animating

sections.caption: 180ms, transform only, no layout work

items: Animate `transform` and `opacity`. They are composited on the GPU and do not force the browser to recalculate layout. Animating `width`, `top` or `margin` reflows the page on every frame.
150–250ms for hover and press feedback. 300ms and up only for entering a new surface, like a dialog.
`ease` or a gentle `cubic-bezier` feels natural; `linear` feels mechanical for UI.
Animate the state change, not the arrival of the element, unless you are deliberately telling a story.

sections.body: Keyframes are for loops and entrances

`transition` interpolates between two states that both exist. `@keyframes` describes a sequence, which is what you want for a loading pulse, a one-off entrance, or an attention nudge. Keep loops slow and low-contrast — a pulsing element in the corner of the eye is a distraction, not a delight.

sections.caption: A slow, quiet loop

sections.body: The guard everyone forgets

Some people set “reduce motion” in their operating system because movement makes them nauseous or triggers migraines. Honour it: keep the state change, drop the travel. One media query covers the whole site.

sections.caption: The reduced-motion guard, written once

sections.title: Focus deserves the same care as hover
sections.body: Use `:focus-visible` so keyboard users see a ring, and never remove an outline without replacing it. A page that only responds to a mouse is half a page.
Check yourself

items: Why is `transform` cheaper than `top`?
What duration feels right for a hover state, and why?
What should happen to a 400ms slide when reduced motion is on?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Animate `transform` and `opacity` only.
150–250ms for feedback; longer only for entering surfaces.
Keyframes for sequences and loops, transitions for state.
Always ship the `prefers-reduced-motion` guard.

drills.prompt: Which query should wrap a large entrance animation?
drills.explain: `prefers-reduced-motion` is the user telling you motion makes them ill. Respect it by replacing movement with an instant change.
hints: Some users get motion sickness.
It is a preference, not a screen size.

drills.prompt: Which property should you animate instead of `width` to stay on the compositor?
drills.explain: `transform` and `opacity` are cheap: the compositor handles them without recalculating layout. Animating `width` forces layout every frame.
hints: It moves or scales the box.
It does not change layout.
